title: AI Changed SaaS (And Nobody Even Realizes)
normalization: Concatenate utf8 segments per caption event; retain event start and duration; whitespace trim only.

segments.text: Somebody told me recently that a buddy
of theirs gave Claude Code the domain
typeform.com
4 hours later Claude Code had built
typeform like exactly typeform. Most
people in SaaS heard that story and
either got panicked or just dismissed
it, but I think both reactions are
wrong. Over the last decade I
bootstrapped three SaaS companies to 30
million in combined ARR and in this
video I want to walk you through what I
think is actually happening here because
from what I'm seeing the entire startup
[music] world is missing the point on
how AI is changing the space. So
Dharmesh Shah, the co-founder and CTO of
HubSpot, posted something that recently
a lot of people agreed with. His
statement was, "I don't see companies
trusting their revenue engine to
something vibe coded over a weekend."
And he's right. Nobody's going to vibe
code HubSpot. I agree with that
completely. The enterprise will keep
buying enterprise software, but that's
not the issue. But the people who think
that framing settles the argument are
looking at the wrong threat. The real
issue isn't whether someone will replace
HubSpot with a weekend project. The real
issue is what changed underneath
everything quietly over the last couple
of years because it used to be pretty
difficult to get software built, not
impossible, but you had to have
engineering talent and that was actually
a massive filter. That filter is
basically gone now. We're entering a
[music] world where almost any code can
be written by almost anyone anywhere in
the world. So there's two facts about
this new world. In this new world
there's two facts that I see. Fact
number one is that it's a far worse
environment for selling software than
before. When building software required
[music] real engineering resources,
there was a natural ceiling on
competition. You needed capital, you
needed talent, and you needed time. The
cost of entry to compete [music] with
any software product has collapsed and
that's not good for the people selling
software. Fact number two is an even
bigger change I see. It takes a one in a
million type founder to take down a
publicly traded SaaS company, someone
with the obsession, the judgment, and
the drive to actually pull off, but that
person has always existed. The question
is how many more of them will be able to
get started now that the engineering
barrier is gone. Drawn in by the hype,
the news cycle, and by the genuine sense
this is the movement to build something.
My answer is that at least 10,000 times
more people will try than tried before
and a few of them will be genuinely
exceptional Elon Musk type guys. That is
why SaaS stocks are getting hurt right
now, not because lovable is replacing
HubSpot with something they vibe coded,
but because the pool of potential
competitors for every SaaS company just
got massively larger overnight. I see a
couple specific problems when it comes
to the future of SaaS. Problem number
one is everyone's going to build
everything at a scale we can't fully
imagine yet. That typeform in 4 hours
story is a sign of what's coming. When
someone can reproduce a year's old SaaS
product in an afternoon, the product
itself is not the moat anymore. Problem
two is every SaaS company is going to
scramble to build agents that do the
work for you. So instead of selling
software that helps you do the job, the
play becomes selling an agent that does
the job for you. This is the Intercom
model. With Fin, instead of selling
software that helps you do a job, sell
an agent that does the job for you and
charge for an outcome. Eoghan McCabe at
Intercom has been very public about this
pivot and every SaaS is eyeing the same
move. Problem number three is that these
agents likely won't carry SaaS margins.
The SaaS model works because once the
software is built, every new customer is
almost pure profit. Agents are
different. There are real token cost per
task and real overhead per interaction.
So you could end up in a situation where
revenue looks fine on paper, but the
margin structure beneath it is getting
worse every month. The only companies
that I think come out on the other side
of this in good shape are ones that
built something genuinely hard to
replicate, a data advantage, a network,
or something that took years that you
can't just vibe code in a weekend. And
that's exactly what I'm trying to build
with R V D B right now, an AI first
company where the product is built
around first-party data that nobody has.
What it does is it pushes the LinkedIn
profiles of your anonymous website
visitors directly to Slack and it takes
about 5 minutes to set up. This way you
can start reaching out to your warmest
leads that you would otherwise leave
without a trace. If you want to try it
out for free, I'll leave the link in the
description below and if you want to see
how I use content in one simple offer to
take R V D B from zero to a million in
16 weeks, watch this video next.
